title: Building HTTP Servers in Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Building an HTTP server in Go is the most common practical task in Go fresher interviews — 'implement a REST endpoint that accepts a JSON body and returns a JSON response' is almost universal. The standard library `net/http` package is powerful enough for production use, and understanding how it works before reaching for Gin or Chi is what interviewers expect freshers to demonstrate.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Two types that make Go HTTP work:

- **`http.ResponseWriter` is where you write the response.** Set headers, set status code, write the body — in that order. Headers and status code must be set before the first `Write` call; after that, they are frozen.
- **`*http.Request` is the entire incoming request.** URL, method, headers, body, query params, path params — all on `r`. The request body is an `io.Reader`, which is why you need `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v)` to parse JSON.
- **A handler is just a function with the right signature.** `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)` — the router calls your function for each matching request. This makes handlers easy to test: call the function directly with `httptest.NewRecorder()` and a constructed `*http.Request`.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **http.HandleFunc** — `http.HandleFunc("/users", handleUsers)` registers a handler on the default ServeMux; pattern must start with `/`
- **http.ListenAndServe** — `http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)` starts the server; nil uses the default ServeMux; blocks until the server exits
- **Request parsing** — `r.URL.Query().Get("name")` for query params; `r.PathValue("id")` for path params (Go 1.22+); `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v)` for JSON body
- **Writing JSON responses** — `w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")` then `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(&v)`; or use `json.Marshal` and `w.Write(data)`
- **Middleware basics** — a function that accepts an `http.Handler` and returns an `http.Handler`; wraps the inner handler with logging, auth, etc.
- **http.Router basics** — Go 1.22+ ServeMux supports method routing: `http.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", handler)`; third-party routers like gorilla/mux or chi for earlier versions or more features
- **Introduction to Gin** — `gin.Default()` creates a router; `r.GET("/users/:id", handler)` registers a route; `c.JSON(200, gin.H{"id": id})` writes JSON; most popular Go web framework

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Headers must be set before WriteHeader** — `w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")` must come before `w.WriteHeader(200)`. Once `WriteHeader` is called, setting headers has no effect and Go logs a warning.
- **Default status is 200 but only after first Write** — if you call `w.Write(data)` without calling `w.WriteHeader`, the status is implicitly 200. Calling `w.WriteHeader(201)` after `w.Write` has no effect.
- **Each HTTP request gets its own goroutine** — `net/http` serves each incoming request in a new goroutine. This is why handlers must be safe for concurrent use — shared state (like an in-memory counter) must be protected with a mutex or atomic.
- **`http.Error` for error responses** — `http.Error(w, "not found", http.StatusNotFound)` is the standard way to return an error response; it sets Content-Type to text/plain and writes the message.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"A Go HTTP server starts with `http.HandleFunc` to register a handler function and `http.ListenAndServe` to start accepting connections. The handler signature is `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)` — I set response headers before writing the status code, and I decode the request JSON body with `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v)`. For middleware, I write a function that accepts an `http.Handler` and returns one — which lets me wrap any handler with logging, authentication, or metrics. Each request runs in its own goroutine, so any shared state in handlers needs to be protected.
